title: I Helped Perform an Exorcism on a Lesbian. Then, I Realized I Was Queer
excerpt: I spent years weaponizing religion to attack LGBTQ people. It was internalized homophobia that fueled it.
content:
In 2000, when I was 16 years old, I remember a young woman standing at the front of our church, speaking into a microphone held by a traveling evangelist.

“I need to be set free; I’m possessed by homosexual demons. Every time I get healed, they come right back, and I sleep with women.”

The traveling evangelist instructed church leaders to come up, lay their hands on the woman, and pray while he cast out the demons. As a youth group leader, I walked up to assist with the exorcism.

“In the name of Jesus Christ, we order that you foul demons leave this woman right now. She is the bride of Christ. Be gone, Satan!” he commanded.

At this point, the evangelist began speaking in tongues. The unintelligible praying grew frenzied. Until finally, the woman fell to the floor. We called it being slain by the Holy Spirit.

“You have been set free from your bondage. As long as you dedicate your life to God, you will no longer struggle with it. You will find a husband and have kids,” he said.

When I took part in the lesbian exorcism, I had only been attending the nondenominational church for a year.

This messaging just confirmed what my family instilled in me growing up: “Jacqui’s a lesbian,” my mom would poke fun at me, though I didn’t think it was funny. “You’re a dyke,” my grandmother told me when I showed up to Thanksgiving dinner wearing an Atlanta Braves hat.

My parents weren’t religious themselves, but our house was so tense that I was looking for any form of salvation. Custody exchanges were so contentious that they were court ordered to take place at the town’s tiny police station. But it didn’t feel safe. The police were rarely there.

I remember one day when they were fighting in the police station parking lot. “Dad, please stop. People at the church can hear you!” I implored.

Mom drove off, leaving my siblings and me with our explosive father.

As I watched her drive away, I noticed people streaming into the fellowship hall of the St. Paul Assembly of God for a potluck.

Dad dragged us over there, saying he didn’t have enough money to buy us dinner.

Inside, the youth pastors greeted us with smiles and sat with us. They seemed happy and nice. It felt safe.

As I continued to struggle with a difficult homelife, church felt safe—and it quickly became my entire life. Whenever the doors were open, I was there. I learned to play guitar and performed in the worship band. Youth group was my favorite part of the week, and I got most of my high school friends to attend. Before long, I became a youth group leader.

I liked that there was a simple answer to all of my problems. What I didn’t realize was conforming to church teachings was causing me to bury my own identity.

As I pushed my secret deep down, my stepdad would make jokes that I was dating my best friend, Sheree, who was also in the Christian club. He was onto something. I was madly in love with her. And she loved me. But we couldn’t admit it.

In my senior year of high school, I was kicked out of the house just after I turned 18. I moved in with my youth pastor and Sheree. We had our own bedrooms, but every night I went to Sheree’s room, and we shared a bed. My big toe rested against her foot in a way that seemed accidental. That was all I could allow myself.

While I was trying to figure out what to do after high school, a traveling evangelist came to our church. He talked about attending the River Bible Institute in Tampa, Florida, where he said God had healed him from bisexuality. I thought this could solve my so-called same-sex attraction and help me find a husband. Sheree and I enrolled together.

At church, men and women couldn’t be alone, not even in the elevator. In the outside world, students weren’t allowed to comingle. One of my guy friends couldn’t come to my birthday party. Premarital sex was forbidden. Even masturbation was a sin.

Pastors at the school decided which students could marry. They were basically arranged marriages.

After graduation, I moved back to St. Paul and began working as a youth pastor at the same church. A couple of months later, I got engaged to the only person I had ever dated. Although I wasn’t attracted to him, I felt like marrying him was God’s will.

It wasn’t long after this that my pastor and I were helping out a congregant who suffered from severe mental illness. She had received a large amount of money and was handing the pastor fistfuls of it, even though she needed every penny. Still, my pastor took the money. I never went back to the church after that.

One day, as the struggle had taken over my life, it was at a women’s Roller Derby party where half the team was naked that I realized there was no question that I was queer.

Thankfully, he was accepting; we began divorce proceedings a few months later. But coming out to the wider world was terrifying. I was used to people making homophobic comments at work, in my family and in public. I was scared coming out would blow up my life. And for a while, it did. I lost my house and my job, and things were unstable. But eventually, I was able to be myself. It felt incredible to release this secret. I immediately bought a bunch of bow ties and wore one every single day. I was relieved every morning when I picked an outfit and didn’t have to struggle with the thought, “Does this make me look gay?”

Therapy has helped immensely with working through the harm I caused my community—and myself—while I was closeted.

Sheree and I stayed in touch, and she accepted me after I came out, even though she was still involved with the church.

Today, I’m 42 years old. And while I still struggle with guilt and shame, I’m happily married to another queer person. I have a wonderful life that I couldn’t have dreamed of when I was repressed, hurting and deeply closeted.

****

In a text to Uncloseted Media, Jacqui’s mother, Margaret, wrote:

I have no issues with what Jacqueline remembers from her childhood. Unfortunately it was not a very good one. I have always supported Jacqui and will always do so. The only thing I can say is that when we know better we do better. My love for my child has never wavered and never will.

Jacqui’s father and the River Bible Institute did not respond to Uncloseted Media’s request for comment.
